484.title: The object exists independent of the mind (4.14–4.17)
484.hook: one photo, two colors, and a very old answer about what's really there
484.howItsDone: Classical Yoga, like Samkhya, is taught as a realist philosophy: the world of nature is real, and practice aims at freeing the mind from the coloring it takes on, not at denying the world.

segments.voice: Yesterday: vasana, the trace of desire with no beginning, which still fades when its supports are gone.

In 2015, a photo of a dress split the internet. Half the people saw blue and black. The other half saw white and gold, and couldn't believe anyone saw anything else. Families argued at dinner. Same photo, same screen, two different dresses. It's an old question in a new outfit: if two minds see one thing so differently, is there really one thing there? Or does each mind make its own world? Patanjali takes that on directly, and he picks a side.
screen: `ONE PHOTO, TWO DRESSES.` → `IS THERE ONE THING THERE AT ALL?` → `PATANJALI PICKS A SIDE.`

segments.voice: Sutra 4.15: vastusamye chittabhedat tayor vibhaktah panthah. The thing being the same, because the minds differ, the two go separate ways. Vastu is the real object out there; chitta is the mind. One dress, two minds, two paths. Patanjali doesn't conclude the dress is imaginary. The difference is in the minds. Sutra 4.14 had already said a thing has its own reality, from the unity of its changes. The next thread pushes further: an object doesn't depend on any one mind. If it did, what would it be when that mind looked away? Would your kitchen vanish while you sleep? Then 4.17 adds the subtle part. A thing is known or not known depending on whether the mind is colored by it. The object is there either way; knowing it is the mind taking on its color, like a clear glass set on red cloth. Why argue this in a book about freedom? The commentators were in conversation with other thinkers of their day, some of them Buddhist philosophers, who held that what we call objects are constructions of mind. Yoga, with its sister school Samkhya, holds that the world is real. That matters for practice. The problem was never that the world is fake. It's the coloring: the wanting, the dread, the story the mind smears onto the tree outside.

segments.voice: Let your eyes rest on one ordinary object near you, a cup, a chair, a plant, and notice the colors your mind lays on it: I like this, this needs washing, someone gave me this. Name each one softly and set it aside. Then let the thing just be there, as itself.
Vastu, the real object out there. For Patanjali, the world is real; minds differ in how they are colored by it.
Your line: realism. The world is real; the coloring comes from the mind. See you tomorrow.

485.title: The mind is not self-luminous (4.18–4.21)
485.hook: a phone screen seems to glow by itself; Patanjali says the mind only seems to
485.howItsDone: In Yoga and Samkhya teaching, the purusha is the unchanging witness and the mind belongs to nature; teachers often use the moon's borrowed light to explain why the mind only seems to shine by itself.

segments.voice: Yesterday: vastu, the real thing out there. One object, two minds, two paths, and the coloring is in the mind.
screen: `REALISM. THE COLORING IS IN THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Look at the moon on a clear night and it seems to shine on its own. It doesn't. Every bit of that silver is borrowed sunlight. Now notice something stranger: you know what you're thinking right now. A thought appears, and it's known. A worry shows up, and it's known. It feels as if the mind glows by itself. Patanjali says that glow is borrowed too, and he names where it comes from.
screen: `THE MOON'S LIGHT IS BORROWED.` → `A THOUGHT APPEARS, AND IT'S KNOWN.` → `BY WHAT?`

segments.voice: Sutra 4.18: the turnings of the mind are always known to their master, the purusha, because the purusha does not change. Purusha is the seer, pure consciousness, the one Patanjali has pointed to since book one. Notice the word always. Every thought, every mood is known, even the ones you'd rather nobody saw. And the reason: the knower doesn't move. A changing thing can't witness all the changes. Then 4.19, short and sharp: na tat svabhasam drishyatvat. It is not self-luminous, because it is seen. The mind is an object, like a cup or a cloud, only subtler. Things that are seen don't light themselves; they're lit. Sutra 4.20 adds that the mind can't know itself and its object in one single act. And 4.21 closes a door. If one mind were known by another mind, you'd need a third to know that one, and a fourth, forever, and memory would be a tangle. So the line has to stop at a seer who isn't a mind at all. Why does that matter on a hard afternoon? If you can see the anxiety, you are not only the anxiety. The weather is real. It's being watched by something that isn't weather.

segments.voice: Let the breath find its own pace, and wait for a thought to come. When it does, don't follow it; just notice, this is known, and the same with a sound, a feeling, a plan for later. You don't have to find the knower; rest in the plain fact that each thing is seen.
Svabhasa, self-luminous — what the mind is not. It is seen, so its light is borrowed, from the purusha, the seer that does not change.

486.title: Discernment ends the sense of "I" (4.25–4.26)
486.hook: the old questions about who you are go quiet, and the mind starts to tilt
486.howItsDone: Teachers of the Yoga Sutras describe viveka, discernment between the seer and the seen, as the turning point of the path; after it, practice is said to become less a struggle and more a natural leaning toward freedom.

segments.voice: Yesterday: svabhasa. The mind isn't self-luminous; it's lit, and known, by the seer.

Who am I, really? Was I someone before this life? What will I be after? These questions tend to arrive at three in the morning, and whole bookshelves are built on them. The old commentary on today's sutra lists questions much like these, then says something surprising. For one person, they stop. Not because they've been answered with a neat paragraph, but because the one asking has seen something that makes them fall quiet.
screen: `WHO AM I, REALLY?` → `THE THREE IN THE MORNING QUESTIONS.` → `FOR ONE PERSON, THEY STOP.`

segments.voice: Sutra 4.25: visheshadarshina atmabhava-bhavana-vinivrittih. For the one who sees the distinction, the cultivation of the sense of self comes to an end. The distinction is the one we've built for days: the mind is seen, the seer sees. Once someone sees that difference plainly, not as an idea but the way you see two different colors, they stop building the self out of the mind's material. Atmabhava-bhavana is a lovely, tangled phrase: the habit of constantly making a self, rehearsing it, feeding it. That habit winds down. Then 4.26 gives a physical image: tada viveka-nimnam kaivalya-pragbharam chittam. Then the mind slopes toward discernment and leans toward freedom. Nimna means low ground, the slope water runs down. Pragbhara means bent forward, weighted toward. Set a marble anywhere inside a bowl, and it finds the bottom without a push. That's the mind now. Freedom isn't an effort anymore. It's downhill. Patanjali stays honest, though. The very next sutra admits that in the gaps, old impressions still throw up other thoughts. The slope doesn't mean the path is finished. It means the ground has changed shape, and everything that falls on it now tends one way.

Nimna, low, sloping ground. Seeing the seer and the seen as different, the habit of building a self out of the mind winds down, and the mind slopes toward freedom.

487.title: The rain-cloud of dharma (4.29)
487.hook: a yogi who wants no interest, even on the highest knowledge, and the cloud that opens
487.tomorrow: The afflictions end; knowledge becomes infinite (4.30–4.31)
487.howItsDone: In the Yoga tradition, dharma-megha samadhi is described as the last stage before kaivalya, reached only when the practitioner seeks nothing, not even from the highest discernment.

segments.voice: Yesterday: nimna, low ground. Once the seer and the mind are seen apart, the mind slopes toward freedom, like a marble in a bowl.

Every app on your phone wants you to collect something. Points, streaks, badges, a gold star for the tenth coffee. It works because we like to see a return. Even a spiritual practice can quietly become that: so much meditation, so much calm, a balance growing in an account somewhere. Patanjali has one word for the person who has stopped keeping that account, even for the highest thing there is. It comes from the world of money, and the sutra it sits in ends with weather.
screen: `POINTS, STREAKS, BADGES, GOLD STARS.` → `A PRACTICE CAN BECOME AN ACCOUNT.` → `A WORD FROM THE WORLD OF MONEY.`

segments.voice: Sutra 4.29: prasankhyane 'py akusidasya sarvatha vivekakhyater dharmameghah samadhih. Even toward the highest discernment, for one who takes no interest, from discernment in every way, comes the samadhi called the cloud of dharma. The money word is kusida: lending at interest, or the interest itself. An akusida charges none. This is someone at the very top of discernment, the clearest seeing there is, who doesn't try to collect on it. No powers from it, no status, not even holding onto it as an achievement. Earlier, Patanjali warned that the powers are obstacles, and that the invitation of the gods should be refused. This is that refusal carried all the way up. When even that last wanting goes, what arrives is dharma-megha. Megha is a cloud, the heavy rain cloud of the monsoon. Commentators read the image in more than one way. Some hear a cloud that rains dharma, pouring down on everything. Others hear a cloud that rains away every last trace of karma. Either way, it's not a trophy. It's weather. It comes when the sky is ready, and it soaks the whole field. The same name, dharma-megha, also appears in Buddhist texts, for the last stage of the bodhisattva's path. Two neighbors, reaching for the same cloud.

488.title: The afflictions end; knowledge becomes infinite (4.30–4.31)
488.hook: when every covering comes off, what's left to know looks small
488.tomorrow: Kaivalya — the power of consciousness resting in itself (4.32–4.34)
488.howItsDone: Commentators on the Yoga Sutras read 4.30–4.31 as the fruit of the whole path: the five kleshas of the second chapter, and the karma they drive, come to an end, and knowledge is uncovered.

segments.voice: Yesterday: akusida, one who takes no interest. To such a person comes the cloud of dharma.

You've lived for years in a room with the curtains closed. You know it well: the lamp, the chair, the stack of books. Then one morning someone pulls every curtain back at once and opens the windows. The room doesn't get bigger, but suddenly it's full of sky: a field outside, a road, a hill you never knew was there. And the lamp, the chair, the books, once the whole world, look like a few small things in a very large light. Patanjali's last chapter has a moment like that.
screen: `A ROOM WITH THE CURTAINS CLOSED.` → `EVERY CURTAIN, PULLED AT ONCE.` → `THE ROOM FULL OF SKY.`

segments.voice: Sutra 4.30: tatah klesha-karma-nivrittih. From that, the afflictions and karma cease. From that means from yesterday's cloud of dharma. Remember the kleshas from the second chapter? Five of them: not-seeing, the I-am feeling, clinging to pleasure, pushing away pain, and clinging to life. Everything on the path since has been about thinning them out. Here, they don't thin. They end. And karma, the whole machinery of seeds and sprouting, ends with them. Then 4.31: tada sarva-avarana-mala-apetasya jnanasya anantyaj jneyam alpam. Then, because knowledge, freed from every covering and impurity, is infinite, what remains to be known is little. Two pictures are tucked inside. Avarana means a covering, like a veil or a lid. Mala means grime, the dust on a lamp's glass. Knowledge was never small. It was covered and smudged. Take off the lid, wipe the glass, and its light reaches without limit. Then that quiet last phrase: jneyam alpam. The knowable is little. Not that the yogi now carries every fact in the world, every name and number. It's proportion. Next to a light without limits, everything that could be known looks like the lamp and the chair in the sunlit room: real, and small.

489.title: Kaivalya — the power of consciousness resting in itself (4.32–4.34)
489.hook: the last thread of the Yoga Sutras, and the small word it ends on
489.howItsDone: Many students of the Yoga Sutras finish a reading of the text by chanting its last sutra, and teachers describe kaivalya as consciousness abiding in its own nature, no longer identified with the mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday: klesha. When the afflictions end, knowledge has no covering, and little remains to be known.

Some books end with a twist, some with a speech. The Yoga Sutras end with one small word: iti. In Sanskrit, iti closes a quotation, a list, or a whole work. It means, more or less, thus. That's what was said. Fifty-nine days ago, this block opened on the first thread: atha yoga-anushasanam, now, the teaching of yoga. Now it closes on thus. Between now and thus sit a hundred and ninety-five threads. Today, the last three.
screen: `SOME BOOKS END WITH A TWIST.` → `THIS ONE ENDS WITH ITI: THUS.` → `FROM NOW TO THUS.`

segments.voice: Sutra 4.32: then, their purpose fulfilled, the gunas finish their sequence of change. The gunas are the three strands of nature, the stuff the mind and the world are woven from. Patanjali has said all along that nature exists for a reason: to give the seer experience, and then freedom. Purpose served, the churning stops. Sutra 4.33 defines that sequence: moments of change, seen only at the end of a transformation, the way you notice a child has grown only when the old shoes don't fit. Then the last thread, 4.34: purushartha-shunyanam gunanam pratiprasavah kaivalyam, svarupa-pratishtha va chiti-shaktir iti. Kaivalya is the return of the gunas to their source, now empty of any purpose for the seer. Or, the power of consciousness established in its own nature. Thus. Ten days ago, at the end of book three, kaivalya was a window wiped clean. Here the same word is said from the seer's side: consciousness no longer confused with the mind's weather. And the second half is the gentlest ending a book could have: svarupa-pratishtha, resting in its own form. All four chapters, from the top. Samadhi Pada: yoga is the stilling of the mind's turnings. Sadhana Pada: the practice, and the eight limbs. Vibhuti Pada: the powers, and the warning about them. Kaivalya Pada: the mind seen clearly, and set down. It began with now. It ends at rest.

segments.voice: For this last sit with Patanjali, do less than ever: let the body be held, let the breath happen without you, and let thoughts be the gunas finishing their work. You aren't reaching for anything; you're resting in what was already here. If you pray, you can offer these sixty days to God, in whatever words are your own.
Kaivalya. In the last thread: the gunas gone back to their source, and the power of consciousness resting in its own nature, the goal the whole Yoga Sutras points toward.
Your line: rest. Tomorrow, a new story begins in a forest: the Ramayana. The Yoga Sutras, done.

490.title: Valmiki and Narada
490.hook: the Ramayana opens with a question: is there anyone like this alive today?
490.carry: many qualities, and hard to find together
490.howItsDone: Some Hindus read Valmiki's Ramayana in Sanskrit or in translation, a set number of chapters a day; the Bala Kanda, the first book, opens with Valmiki's question and Narada's answer.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kaivalya, and the Yoga Sutras' last word, iti, thus. The book that began with now ends at rest.

For the next six months, give or take, we're reading one story, in order, a little each day, like a serial: the Ramayana, as Valmiki tells it, book by book. You may know the outline already: a prince, an exile, a kidnapping, a war, a homecoming. But Valmiki doesn't start with a battle or a birth. He starts in a quiet forest hermitage, with one man asking a visitor a question about a person. Who, today, is good all the way through?
screen: `SIX MONTHS. ONE STORY. IN ORDER.` → `NOT A BATTLE. A HERMITAGE.` → `WHO IS GOOD ALL THE WAY THROUGH?`

segments.voice: The Ramayana's first verse sets the scene. Tapah-svadhyaya-niratam: devoted to discipline and study. That describes Narada, the wandering sage, best of those who know how to speak. The one asking is Valmiki, a hermit himself. His question is a list, and it's worth hearing how long it is. Is there anyone in the world right now who is virtuous, and strong, who knows what's right, who's grateful, truthful, firm in his promises? Someone of good conduct, kind to every living being, learned, capable, good to look at? Someone who has mastered himself and conquered his anger, who shines, who envies no one, and yet whom even the gods fear when he's roused in battle? Tradition counts sixteen qualities in that question. Narada answers honestly: those are many qualities, and hard to find together. But I know one. Born in the line of Ikshvaku, people call him Rama. So the whole epic opens as an answer to a question about character, and the story that follows is the evidence. Now the week, from the top, the last days of Patanjali. One object, two minds, two paths. The mind lit by the seer. Discernment, and the mind sloping toward freedom. The cloud of dharma. Little left to know. Kaivalya, rest. And today, a new question in a forest: is anyone like this alive?
screen: `A HERMIT ASKS A WANDERING SAGE.` · `SIXTEEN QUALITIES IN ONE QUESTION.` · `NARADA: I KNOW ONE. RAMA.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `TAPAḤSVĀDHYĀYANIRATAM.`

segments.voice: Think of one person you've known, living or gone, who had some of Valmiki's list: truthful, kind to every living being, slow to anger, grateful. Not perfect, just good in a way you remember; let their face come, and breathe with one of their qualities resting in your chest. If you pray, you can give thanks for them.
Narada, the wandering sage who answers Valmiki's question. The Ramayana begins as their conversation about character.
